sections.title: Cellular organization
sections.text:
The cell is the basic organizational unit of life. Organisms may consist of one cell or many specialized cells. Cell theory holds that living organisms are composed of cells, cells are fundamental units of structure and function, and new cells arise from existing cells. A virus has genetic material and can evolve, but lacks independent cellular metabolism and reproduces using host machinery; it is not an ordinary cell.

All cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic information and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells, including bacteria and archaea, lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and internal membrane-bound compartments. “Prokaryotic” does not mean biologically unsuccessful or chemically inactive: prokaryotes perform extraordinarily diverse metabolic processes.

| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nuclear organization | DNA in a nucleoid region | Most DNA enclosed in nucleus |
| Internal compartments | No typical membrane-bound nucleus or eukaryotic organelles | Extensive membrane-bound organelles |
| Ribosomes | Present | Present in cytosol and certain organelles |
| Typical division | Binary fission | Mitosis; meiosis in sexual life cycles |
| Examples | Bacteria and archaea | Animals, plants, fungi and diverse protists |

Cell size is limited partly by transport. As a roughly spherical cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area, making exchange across its surface less adequate relative to internal demand. Small size, folded membranes and specialized transport systems help overcome this constraint. Microscopy reveals structure, while biochemical experiments are needed to establish what structures actually do.

sections.title: Organelles and division of labour
sections.text:
The nucleus contains chromosomes and helps regulate gene expression. Its envelope has pores controlling exchange. The nucleolus participates in producing ribosomal components. Ribosomes translate messenger RNA into polypeptides; they can be free in the cytosol or associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum. Ribosomes are not enclosed by their own membrane.

The rough endoplasmic reticulum processes many proteins destined for secretion or membranes. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum participates in lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium handling in appropriate cells. The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts cargo received through the endomembrane system. Vesicles transport material between compartments and to the cell surface. A secreted protein commonly follows ribosome at rough ER → ER processing → Golgi → secretory vesicle → exocytosis. The Golgi does not read mRNA to synthesize the original polypeptide.

Mitochondria participate in aerobic metabolism and ATP production. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae. Lysosomes contain enzymes for degradation in acidic compartments; peroxisomes participate in selected oxidative reactions and peroxide metabolism. The cytoskeleton provides organization, transport tracks and mechanical support. [OpenStax: eukaryotic cells](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells).

Typical plant cells have cellulose-rich walls, a large central vacuole and, in photosynthetic tissues, chloroplasts. Typical animal cells lack these structures but also have mitochondria, membranes and ribosomes. Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts: many root cells do not. Cell walls provide support outside the membrane; they do not replace the selective membrane barrier.

sections.title: Membrane transport and osmotic balance
sections.text:
The plasma membrane contains a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. Phospholipids have water-interacting heads and hydrophobic tails, causing them to organize into a barrier in water. Membranes remain dynamic rather than completely rigid. Cholesterol in many animal-cell membranes modifies molecular packing, permeability and fluidity across different temperatures.

Simple diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient through random molecular motion. Small nonpolar molecules cross lipid membranes relatively readily. Facilitated diffusion uses channels or carriers but still follows the relevant gradient. Active transport uses energy to move material against its electrochemical gradient. The sodium–potassium pump normally uses ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, supporting ionic gradients. Secondary active transport uses energy already stored in another gradient. [OpenStax: active transport](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/5-3-active-transport).

Osmosis is net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane driven by differences in water potential. Tonicity describes a solution's effect on cell volume and depends especially on solutes that do not freely cross the membrane. In a hypertonic solution, a cell tends to lose water; in a hypotonic solution, it tends to gain water. Plant walls resist expansion and permit turgor pressure. Severe water loss can pull the membrane away from the wall, producing plasmolysis. Isotonic conditions do not mean water molecules stop moving; opposing fluxes approximately balance.

Large materials can enter by endocytosis or leave by exocytosis. These vesicle processes differ from a molecule simply passing through a protein channel. Membrane transport connects cell biology with intestinal absorption, kidney function, nerve signalling and water treatment by engineered membranes.

sections.title: DNA, genes and replication
sections.text:
DNA stores hereditary information in sequences of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base. In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine. The strands run in opposite chemical directions. A gene is a functional unit of genetic information whose expression produces RNA and, for protein-coding genes, a polypeptide through additional steps.

Before cell division, DNA is copied. The strands separate, each provides a template and enzymes synthesize complementary strands. Each resulting double helix contains one parental and one new strand, hence semiconservative replication. DNA polymerases extend existing strands in a defined direction; other enzymes help unwind DNA, supply primers and join fragments. Copying is highly accurate but not error-free, and repair systems correct many errors. [OpenStax: DNA replication](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/14-3-basics-of-dna-replication).

A mutation is a change in genetic sequence. It may alter a protein, affect gene regulation, have little detectable effect or be harmful or beneficial in a particular environment. Because several codons can specify the same amino acid, a base substitution may be synonymous. Such a change does not alter that amino acid, although it can sometimes affect other aspects of expression.

sections.title: Gene expression and cell division
sections.text:
Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template. In eukaryotes, a protein-coding transcript is commonly processed before mature messenger RNA reaches ribosomes. During translation, transfer RNAs match anticodons with mRNA codons and deliver amino acids. Ribosomes link amino acids into a polypeptide, which folds and may undergo further modification.

```text
DNA sequence → transcription → RNA
Protein-coding mRNA → translation at ribosome → polypeptide → functional protein
```

DNA replication copies the genome; transcription produces RNA; translation produces polypeptide. Confusing these processes obscures how inheritance and cell function are related. Many functional RNAs are not translated at all.

Mitosis distributes duplicated chromosomes into daughter nuclei and commonly supports growth and repair. Meiosis reduces chromosome number and introduces genetic variation through recombination and chromosome assortment in sexual life cycles. Fertilization restores the diploid chromosome complement. Cell-cycle regulation prevents uncontrolled proliferation; failure of regulation contributes to cancer. A tissue's behaviour therefore depends on both its genetic information and the controlled use of that information.

**From organelles to tissue specialization.** Cells share many basic structures but allocate them differently. A cell that secretes large amounts of protein commonly has substantial rough ER and Golgi activity. A cell with high aerobic energy demand may have many mitochondria. Mature mammalian red blood cells lose their nuclei and mitochondria during development, illustrating why a typical-cell diagram does not describe every specialized cell. Function is explained by both the presence and relative development of structures.

**The consequences of a transport defect.** If an ion channel changes activity, membrane voltage and cell signalling can change. If a glucose transporter fails, nutrient uptake can become inadequate despite glucose being present outside. If lysosomal processing is defective, substrates can accumulate within cells. These examples show why knowing an organelle's name is insufficient: the relevant question is how a specific molecular function supports the larger cellular system.

**Genotype, environment and phenotype.** Genotype describes genetic constitution, while phenotype describes observable characteristics arising from genetic information interacting with environment and development. Gene expression can vary among tissues even when most cells carry the same genome. A liver cell and a neuron differ because they use different regulatory programmes, not because one necessarily lacks all genes used by the other. Mutation, inheritance and regulation must therefore be distinguished when explaining a biological trait.

questions.prompt: A cell produces a protein intended for secretion outside the cell. Which pathway is typically involved?

options.C: Rough ER → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicles

questions.explanation: Many secretory proteins are synthesized on rough-ER-associated ribosomes and processed through the Golgi and vesicle pathway.

questions.prompt: A typical plant cell is placed in a strongly hypertonic solution. Which response may occur?

options.A: Water leaves the cell and the plasma membrane may pull away from the wall
options.D: The cell necessarily increases its turgor pressure indefinitely

questions.explanation: Osmosis can remove water from the cell, causing loss of turgor and plasmolysis.

questions.prompt: A ribosome is actively translating a messenger RNA molecule. What is its immediate principal product?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into polypeptides according to the mRNA codon sequence.

questions.prompt: Why do membrane cholesterol molecules influence fluidity in many animal cells?

options.B: They affect phospholipid packing and membrane physical behavior
options.C: They make the membrane entirely rigid at all temperatures
options.D: They transform membrane proteins into DNA

questions.explanation: Cholesterol modulates membrane packing and permeability, buffering fluidity across temperature ranges.

questions.prompt: The sodium–potassium ATPase typically transports which ion combination per ATP hydrolyzed?

options.A: Two sodium out and three potassium in
options.B: Three sodium in and three potassium out
options.C: Three sodium out and two potassium in
options.D: One proton out and two calcium in

questions.explanation: The pump moves three Na+ ions out and two K+ ions in, helping maintain electrochemical gradients.

questions.prompt: What directly powers mitochondrial ATP synthase during normal oxidative phosphorylation?

options.A: The proton electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.B: Direct binding of sunlight to hemoglobin
options.D: Diffusion of glucose through the nucleus

questions.explanation: The electron-transport chain helps establish a proton-motive force, which ATP synthase couples to ATP formation.

questions.prompt: A protein synthesized for delivery to a lysosome passes through the Golgi apparatus. One important Golgi role is:

options.A: Replacing the protein with pure lipid
options.D: Modifying and sorting molecular cargo toward suitable destinations

questions.explanation: The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins and lipids, including cargo destined for endomembrane compartments.

questions.prompt: A DNA base substitution changes an mRNA codon but does not change the encoded amino acid. This is:

options.A: A chromosome deletion in every case
options.B: A mutation that necessarily stops translation
options.C: A synonymous or silent coding substitution

questions.explanation: Genetic-code degeneracy permits multiple codons to specify the same amino acid, although some synonymous changes can still affect regulation.

questions.prompt: Each daughter double-stranded DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. This describes:
questions.explanation: Semiconservative replication uses each parental strand as a template for a newly synthesized complementary strand.

analytical.prompt: Explain how DNA, enzymes, mitochondria and cellular membranes cooperate to maintain life. What can happen when one component becomes defective?
analytical.answer_html:
Introduction

Cellular function depends on the coordinated activities of genetic information, protein synthesis, chemical reactions, energy conversion and selective transport.

Genetic information

DNA contains the instructions needed to produce RNA and many proteins. Transcription produces RNA using a DNA template. Translation assembles amino acids into polypeptides according to messenger RNA.

Enzyme function

Most enzymes are proteins with structures that enable catalytic activity. They lower the activation-energy barrier of biochemical reactions. Metabolic pathways depend on many enzymes functioning together.

Energy production

Mitochondria perform major stages of aerobic energy metabolism in eukaryotic cells. The electron-transport chain helps establish a proton electrochemical gradient. ATP synthase uses this gradient to support ATP production.

Membrane transport

The plasma membrane controls the movement of ions, nutrients and other molecules. Transport proteins maintain electrochemical conditions necessary for signaling and metabolism.

Consequences of defects

A gene alteration may change a protein's structure or expression. An enzyme defect can block or impair a metabolic pathway. A mitochondrial defect may reduce energy availability. A membrane transporter defect can disturb cellular chemical balance.

Conclusion

Genetic information, protein function, membrane transport and energy metabolism form an interconnected system. Cellular disease may arise when defects in one component disrupt the performance of the others.
